chapter.title: Optical, Photographic, Cinematographic, Measuring, Checking, Precision, Medical or Surgical Instruments and Apparatus; Parts and Accessories Thereof

page.h1: HTS Chapter 90: Optical, Photographic, Cinematographic, Measuring, Checking, Precision, Medical or Surgical Instruments and Apparatus; Parts and Accessories Thereof — U.S. Export Rules & Ways to Pay Less Abroad

seo.title: U.S. Medical Device & Instrument Export Rules: FDA & Controls (HTS Ch. 90) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What U.S. exporters of medical devices, lasers, optics, navigation and measuring instruments must do before shipping: FDA export rules and certificates, Commerce licences, ITAR and Russia rules.

intro: A U.S. exporter of instruments takes the same five steps as every exporter. For medical devices, the agency that matters is the **FDA**: a device legally marketed in the U.S. can be exported, an unapproved one only under sections 801(e)(1) or 802 of the FD&C Act, and importing countries often ask for an FDA export certificate. Most instruments are EAR99 and need no export licence, but lasers, thermal-imaging cameras, image sensors, gyroscopes and satellite-navigation receivers, some inspection machines and military optics are controlled, and nearly every heading in this chapter has lines on the Russia and Belarus licence lists.

steps.title: Find the Schedule B number
steps.whatToDo: Look up the 10-digit Schedule B number for each product with the Census Bureau's free search tool. Its first six digits are the same as the HS code every country uses, so it also tells you which line of the buyer's tariff applies. The U.S. import (HTS) number and the Schedule B number match only to six digits.
steps.when: Every export. It goes on the export filing (the last step) and on the commercial invoice.
steps.chapterNote: Medical, surgical and dental instruments (9018) were 35% of 2025 exports; the largest line was 9018.90 (other medical, surgical or dental instruments, $18.57B), then 9018.39 (catheters and cannulae, $7.96B). Medical-device Schedule B numbers are 10 digits and can differ from the HTS beyond six.

steps.title: Screen the buyer and everyone in the deal
steps.whatToDo: Check the buyer, the end user and any agent against the Consolidated Screening List. It combines the Commerce lists (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified, Military End-User), the State Department lists and the Treasury (OFAC) sanctions lists of parties you may not deal with, or may deal with only under a licence.
steps.when: Every export, before you accept the order.
steps.chapterNote: Screen the end user, not only the distributor: hospitals, police and military buyers appear on the lists, and dual-use items such as thermal imagers and navigation equipment are the usual diversion targets.

steps.title: Check whether you need an export licence
steps.whatToDo: Find the product's Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) on the Commerce Control List. Most goods are not listed and are EAR99. For a listed ECCN, look up the destination on the Commerce Country Chart under each reason for control: an X means a licence is needed unless a licence exception applies. Even EAR99 goods need a licence for embargoed countries and for restricted end users or end uses.
steps.when: Every export of goods subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
steps.chapterNote: Most medical devices and many instruments are EAR99. Controlled items include lasers (ECCN 6A005), thermal-imaging cameras and image sensors (6A002, 6A003), certain optical components (6A004), gyroscopes (7A002), satellite-navigation receivers (7A005) and some dimensional-inspection machines (2B006); semiconductor inspection equipment may fall under Category 3.

steps.title: Check sanctions on the destination
steps.whatToDo: Check the destination against OFAC's sanctions programs and the EAR's embargo rules. Cuba, Iran and North Korea have country-wide rules, and Syria still needs a Commerce licence for most items; Russia and Belarus need a licence for any item with an ECCN. Several programs have special permissions for food and medicine.
steps.when: Exports to a sanctioned or embargoed country, or to a listed person anywhere.
steps.chapterNote: Russia and Belarus: a Commerce licence is required for 143 six-digit Chapter 90 codes in Supplement No. 4 to 15 CFR Part 746 — nearly every heading from 9001 to 9033 — and one in Supplement 5. Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Syria are covered by country-wide rules; some programs have special permissions for medical devices.

steps.title: File the export in AES (Electronic Export Information)
steps.whatToDo: You (the U.S. principal party in interest) or your freight forwarder file the EEI in the Automated Export System — free through ACE AESDirect — and put the confirmation number (ITN) on the shipping documents. File at least 24 hours before an ocean shipment is loaded, 2 hours before a flight departs, or 1 hour before a truck reaches the border. Not filing can cost a civil penalty of up to $17,412 per violation.
steps.when: When one Schedule B number in one shipment to one buyer is worth over $2,500, and at any value when the shipment needs a Commerce licence or a DEA permit or declaration, or ships an EAR item to Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Syria, or a Commerce Control List item to China, Russia or Venezuela.
steps.chapterNote: Instruments are high-value, so most shipments exceed $2,500 per Schedule B number and need an EEI filing; a licence for a controlled item requires a filing at any value.

rules.title: Medical devices: a device legally marketed in the U.S. can be exported; an unapproved device can be exported only if it meets FD&C Act section 801(e)(1) (labeled for export, not sold in the U.S., meets the importing country's requirements) or section 802 (Class II or III devices sent to listed countries after a notification)

citations.label: 21 U.S.C. 381 (FD&C Act section 801: imports and exports)
21 U.S.C. 382 (FD&C Act section 802: exports of certain unapproved products)

rules.title: Export certificates: FDA issues a Certificate to Foreign Government (CFG) for devices legally marketed in the U.S. and exported from the U.S., which many importing countries ask for; export permit letters and simple notifications carry no fee

citations.label: FDA: exporting medical devices (certificates, permit letters and notifications)

rules.title: Investigational devices: obtain FDA's prior approval of the export under section 801(e) of the FD&C Act, or comply with section 802 (21 CFR 812.18(b))

Lasers, thermal-imaging cameras, image sensors and optical components: ECCNs 6A002 (optical sensors), 6A003 (cameras), 6A004 (optical equipment) and 6A005 (lasers) need a licence for the destinations on the Country Chart

citations.label: Commerce Control List (15 CFR 774 Supp. 1), Category 6

rules.title: Gyroscopes and satellite-navigation receiving equipment: ECCN 7A002 (gyros and angular-rate sensors) and 7A005 (satellite navigation receivers) in Category 7 are controlled for national-security and missile-technology reasons

citations.label: Commerce Control List (15 CFR 774 Supp. 1), Category 7

rules.title: Dimensional inspection and measuring systems, such as coordinate measuring machines: ECCN 2B006; semiconductor wafer inspection and metrology tools may fall under the Category 3 controls on chip-making equipment

citations.label: Commerce Control List (15 CFR 774 Supp. 1), Categories 2 and 3

rules.agency: State Department, Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC)
rules.title: Night-vision, laser, imaging and guidance equipment designed for military use: U.S. Munitions List Category XII, which needs a State Department licence
Russia and Belarus: a licence is required for the instruments on the HS-code lists in Supplements No. 4 and 5 to Part 746 (15 CFR 746.8)

groups.label: Optical fibers, contact lenses, spectacle lenses & unmounted optics
Mounted lenses, filters, prisms & mirrors for instruments
Binoculars, telescopes & astronomical instruments
groups.note: Night-vision binoculars and similar optics can be controlled under ECCN 6A002 or the ITAR; ordinary binoculars and telescopes are generally not controlled.

groups.label: Still cameras, flash units & parts
groups.note: Cameras with certain infrared or high-speed sensors can be controlled under ECCN 6A003; ordinary cameras are generally not controlled.

groups.label: Photo lab equipment, negatoscopes & projection screens
Lasers, rifle scopes, magnifiers & other optical devices
groups.note: Lasers are controlled under ECCN 6A005 by power and wavelength; rifle scopes and weapon sights can fall under the ITAR or the Commerce firearms controls.

groups.label: Compasses, autopilots & navigational instruments
groups.note: Gyroscopes and inertial navigation equipment are controlled under ECCN 7A002; ordinary compasses are generally not controlled.

groups.label: Surveying, rangefinders, weather & geophysical instruments
groups.note: Satellite-navigation surveying receivers (ECCN 7A005) and laser rangefinders can be controlled.

groups.label: Drafting instruments, calipers, micrometers & measuring tapes
Medical, surgical, dental & veterinary instruments (incl. syringes, catheters, ECG, ultrasound, MRI)
groups.note: Most medical devices are EAR99 for export control; the FDA rules decide what may be exported and what certificate the importing country will ask for.

groups.label: Massage & mechano-therapy apparatus, oxygen therapy, ventilators & CPAP
Orthopedic devices, implants, artificial joints, hearing aids & pacemakers
groups.note: Implants, orthopedic devices and hearing aids are regulated medical devices; check the importing country's registration before shipping.

groups.label: X-ray, CT & radiotherapy apparatus and X-ray tubes
groups.note: X-ray, CT and radiotherapy apparatus are regulated medical devices.

groups.label: Flow meters, level gauges & pressure instruments
Laboratory analysis instruments: spectrometers, chromatographs, analyzers
Oscilloscopes, multimeters, electrical test & radiation-measuring instruments
Measuring & inspection machines: CMMs, wafer and mask inspection, test benches
groups.note: Coordinate measuring machines are in ECCN 2B006, and wafer inspection tools (9031.41, $2.60B in 2025) can fall under chip-making equipment controls.

groups.label: Parts & accessories not specified elsewhere in Chapter 90

savings.title: Claim the free-trade-agreement rate abroad
savings.saves: The partner country's tariff on qualifying U.S. goods — often 0% instead of its normal rate.
savings.appliesTo: Goods that meet the agreement's rules of origin, shipped to one of the 20 U.S. free-trade-agreement partners: Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Oman, Panama, Peru and Singapore.
savings.document: A certification of origin from the exporter, producer or importer, which the buyer uses to claim the rate at import. For USMCA there is no set form, but it must contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A.
savings.caveat: Whoever certifies must be able to back it up: for USMCA, a U.S. exporter or producer keeps origin records for at least 5 years, gives CBP a copy on request and tells buyers promptly about errors. Check the product's rule of origin and the partner's rate in the FTA Tariff Tool first.

savings.title: Get U.S. duty back on imported inputs (drawback)
savings.saves: 99% of the U.S. import duties, taxes and fees paid on goods or materials that are exported, or used to make the goods you export.
savings.appliesTo: Imported goods exported unused, and imported materials used to make an exported product (or, under the substitution rules, goods of the same kind).
savings.document: An electronic drawback claim in ACE, filed within 5 years of the import date, with the import and export records that tie the two together.
savings.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refunded, and CBP takes no paper claims. The refund is on U.S. duties only; it does not lower the buyer's tariff.

disclaimer: This page summarizes U.S. export rules to help you find the right regulation; it is not legal advice. Rules change and depend on the exact product, buyer and destination — check the cited regulation and the agency before you ship.
